meta.title: Grok Bot Isn't Your Coder. It's Your Engineering Manager. (v3, blueprint)

lines.text: It's eight a.m. You haven't touched your laptop since last night.
But your bot has been busy. Nine pull requests ready for review. Four already merged.
And one that needs a human. That's you.
This isn't a fantasy. In xAI's own engineering guide, one engineer describes managing fifteen cloud coding agents by hand.
Now their bots manage more than two hundred of them at the same time.
The difference isn't a better prompt. It's the job you give Grok Bot.
Most people make it the coder. The people shipping the most make it the manager.

items.text: Hands code to a cloud agent
Watches the PR until it's green

lines.text: Here's the trap. Grok Bot has a terminal and a browser on a cloud computer, so yes, it can write code.
But every bot shares that one machine and its logins, and you'd be reviewing a chat transcript instead of a diff.
So give it the job it's built for. It hands the code to a cloud agent, demands proof, and watches the pull request until it's green.

scenes.label: Two loops
scenes.title: The outer loop feeds the inner loop

els.text:
cloud agent
one repo · one task

lines.text: Think of it as two loops. The inner loop is a coding agent: one repo, one task, real tests.
The outer loop is Grok Bot. It reads Slack, the bug tracker and your messages, and turns them into that one task.
The brainstorming and the dead ends stay outside. The agent only ever sees a clean brief.

Bots can now hand off coding tasks to Cursor, manage pull requests through GitHub, and share video demos of what they build.

highlight.text: The bot runs the *loop*. You own the *merge*.

lines.text: So split the work. The bot gathers context and writes the brief. The agent edits code and runs the tests.
The bot checks the proof and keeps going overnight. And merging stays with you, unless the change is genuinely low risk.

data.title: One bot, one domain
data.sub: Set up the team before the work

lines.text: Chapter one. Set up the team before you hand it any work.
In the official guide, each engineer bot owns one area: iOS, the desktop app and its CI, infrastructure, Android, and the bot harness itself.
They can work across areas, but each has its own memory and limited context, so they're sharpest where they own the specs.

scenes.label: The role
scenes.title: Write the role in three layers

data.code:
# Desktop Bot · desktop app + CI

## Rules (never change)
- Never push to main. Never touch deploy keys.
- Every task ships with proof: tests + screenshots.
- Stop and ask before anything irreversible.

## Job (owned)
- Own the desktop client and its CI pipeline.
- Keep CI under 12 minutes.

## Current assignment
- Fix the Windows Arm64 onboarding crash.

lines.text: Then write each bot's role in three layers.
Rules that never change. The job it owns. And the current assignment, which you can swap without touching the rules.

scenes.label: Before you sign in
scenes.title: One computer, shared by every bot

els.title: A fork or scoped token. *No deploy keys.*
Secure input only. Never in chat.

els.text: docs.x.ai · Grok Bot computer and security docs

lines.text: One warning before you connect anything. Every bot on your account shares one cloud computer, with the same files and logins.
Separate bots are not a security boundary. So give them a fork or a scoped token. Never deploy keys.
Enter secrets through the secure input, never in chat, and keep them out of slash workspace, where every bot can read them.
Chapter two. The handoff.

scenes.label: In practice
scenes.title: One line in, a full brief out

messages.text: Onboarding crashes on small iPhones since yesterday's release. P1.
On it. 3 Slack reports + the crash trace. It's the new layout on 320pt screens.
Proof required: *before/after screenshots* on iPhone SE, and *e2e green*.

lines.text: Here's what that looks like. You drop a one-line bug report.
The bot pulls the Slack thread and the crash trace, then starts a Cursor cloud agent with the right skills loaded.
And it says, up front, what proof it expects back.

data.code:
## Task
Fix the onboarding crash on screens under 375pt.

## Context
3 Slack reports · crash trace #8812 · since v4.12

## Skills
/ios-best-practices  /run-ios-e2e

## Proof expected
- Before vs after screenshots, iPhone SE
- e2e suite green

## Stop and ask if
- The fix touches auth or payments

lines.text: That brief is the whole game. The task. The context it already gathered.
Which skills to load. What proof to bring back. And when to stop and ask, instead of guessing.

els.title: Fix the crash on screens under 375pt
els.body: Proof: before/after on iPhone SE · e2e green

lines.text: That's the outer loop protecting the inner one. The messy thinking stays with the bot. The agent gets a clean task.
Chapter three. Close the loop.
The single most important idea in the guide: give the agent a complete feedback loop.
The agent works and attaches proof. The bot checks it, and if it doesn't match the request, it pushes back.
Round after round, until the goal is met. Not until the agent says it's done.

checks.text: Fixed on iPhone SE · e2e green

lines.text: Cloud agents can attach screenshots, and the bot really looks at them.
Here, the button is still clipped on the smallest screen, so it goes back to the agent instead of to you.
Round two. Fixed, tests green, verified.

scenes.label: Let it drive
scenes.title: Give the agent the whole stack

lines.text: For that loop to work, the agent has to drive the stack end to end: launch a dev build, click through it, capture the result.
Chrome DevTools for the web. A CLI for services. Accessibility APIs for the iOS simulator.
And when it figures out a flow, have it package that into a reusable repo skill.
So here's the rule. If the agent can't check its own work, it can't work without you.
Chapter four. Scale past the context window.

scenes.label: Every 30 minutes
scenes.title: A shared board the bots maintain

lines.text: Long chats scroll away, so the bots keep a shared database of every pull request.
Every thirty minutes, they sweep it: bug-bot comments, failing CI, merge conflicts.
Anything off goes straight back to the agent, and the row moves back to Working. Clean ones move to Ready for review.
Clean PRs get an automatic code review. If the review is highly confident and the blast radius is low, it merges on its own.
Everything else waits for you, with the proof attached, so your review takes minutes instead of an afternoon.

lines.text: Here's what the team behind Grok Bot reports. One engineer shipped more than two thousand pull requests in a month.

data.title: The night shift
data.sub: Routines that work while you sleep

lines.text: Chapter five. The night shift.
Routines turn all of this into a schedule. Every thirty minutes, the PR sweep.
At three a.m., the nightly audit: dead code, load time, bundle size. At five, the ops bot meets every engineer bot.
And at eight, you wake up to a list of PRs that are ready to merge.

els.code:
nightly-audits:
  - name: security-sweep
    at: "03:00"
  - name: ci-build-time
    at: "03:20"
  - name: i18n-gaps
    at: "03:40"
  - name: ios-desktop-parity
    at: "04:00"
  - name: catch-up-summary
    at: "07:30"

lines.text: The guide lists audits worth stealing.
Security sweeps. CI build time. Missing translations. Parity between your iOS and desktop apps. And a catch-up summary of everything merged in the last day.

els.text: “You have six hours tonight. Build whatever you want. Have *fun*.”

lines.text: And their favorite nightly prompt of all. You have six hours tonight. Build whatever you want. Have fun.
A few details from the docs will save you money.
Schedules must be at least five minutes apart. Pressing Test does real work. And never use a broad trigger, like every new message.
If you're away for a long time, routines can be paused until you respond.

els.text: Checkout is failing on Android. *This is P0.*

els.title: P0 watch started
els.body: checking the agent's transcript every 5 min

els.text: Agent was retrying a flaky test. Steered it to the real failure: *payment SDK timeout*.

lines.text: One more trick. When something is truly urgent, tell the bot it's P0.
It starts a temporary routine that checks the agent's transcript every five minutes, and steers it when it wastes time.
It burns tokens fast, so save it for real emergencies.
Chapter six. Keep the org sharp.
The one bot that writes no code is the ops bot. When an engineer bot makes a mistake, the ops bot runs a postmortem.
It finds the root cause, updates the playbook, and announces the change to every bot. Then it repeats it in a daily one-on-one, so nobody forgets.
And when a bot struggles, treat it like a talented intern. Ask it to do its homework, and to study how your best engineers do the job.

scenes.label: Honest limits
scenes.title: When not to use Grok Bot

items.sub: fixed rules → a script or CI job

verdict.text: Use it where *judgment* beats a cron job

lines.text: Now the honest part. Don't use it for deterministic jobs. If the inputs and rules are fixed, write a script or a CI job.
Keep it out of hard real-time paths. Don't treat separate bots as separate trust zones. And if you need to choose the exact model, there's no model picker.

items.sub: fix the process, not the output

gate.text: Then turn on the nightly audit

lines.text: Here's how to start this week. Create one engineer bot for one domain. Write a handoff skill that demands proof.
Run one real task by hand, and fix the process, not just the output. Then add the thirty-minute PR sweep.
Only when that runs clean for a week, turn on the nightly audit.
Don't ask Grok Bot to write your code. Ask it to run your loop.
